AI.method: VGM2Robot uses vision-language models (VLMs) to automatically extract compositional constraints from language instructions, then applies these constraints in two stages: (1) constraint-guided rollout selection to filter VGM rollouts for physical plausibility, and (2) constraint-based trajectory optimization to refine robot trajectories and correct retargeting errors.
AI.result: The method improves overall success rate by 43.3 percentage points over the strongest baseline on six real-robot manipulation tasks requiring precise, constraint-sensitive execution, without any task-specific training data.
AI.conclusion: VGM2Robot demonstrates that combining VGMs with VLMs' structured spatial reasoning capabilities enables effective zero-shot robotic manipulation by addressing physical plausibility and retargeting error challenges through compositional constraint extraction and application.

title: The EpisTwin: A Knowledge Graph-Grounded Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Personal AI
summary: Personal Artificial Intelligence is currently hindered by the fragmentation of user data across isolated silos. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation offers a partial remedy, its reliance on unstructured vector similarity fails to capture the latent semantic topology and temporal dependencies essential for holistic sensemaking. We introduce EpisTwin, a neuro-symbolic framework that grounds generative reasoning in a verifiable, user-centric Personal Knowledge Graph. EpisTwin leverages Multimodal Language Models to lift heterogeneous, cross-application data into semantic triples. At inference, EpisTwin enables complex reasoning over the personal semantic graph via an agentic coordinator that combines Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Online Deep Visual Refinement, dynamically re-grounding symbolic entities in their raw visual context. We also introduce PersonalQA-71-100, a synthetic benchmark designed to simulate a realistic user's digital footprint and evaluate EpisTwin performance. Our framework demonstrates robust results across a suite of state-of-the-art judge models, offering a promising direction for trustworthy Personal AI.

AI.tldr: EpisTwin is a neuro-symbolic framework that creates Personal Knowledge Graphs from fragmented user data to enable trustworthy reasoning for Personal AI, outperforming traditional vector-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Current Personal AI suffers from data fragmentation across isolated silos. Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approaches rely on unstructured vector similarity, which fails to capture latent semantic topology and temporal dependencies needed for holistic sensemaking.
AI.method: EpisTwin uses Multimodal Language Models to transform heterogeneous, cross-application data into semantic triples, constructing a verifiable Personal Knowledge Graph. At inference, it employs an agentic coordinator combining Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Online Deep Visual Refinement to dynamically re-ground symbolic entities in their raw visual context.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates robust performance across state-of-the-art judge models on PersonalQA-71-100, a synthetic benchmark simulating realistic user digital footprints, showing promising results for trustworthy Personal AI.
AI.conclusion: EpisTwin offers a neuro-symbolic approach that grounds generative reasoning in verifiable Personal Knowledge Graphs, addressing limitations of traditional vector-based methods and providing a promising direction for trustworthy Personal AI systems.

title: Multi-Robot Trajectory Planning via Constrained Bayesian Optimization and Local Cost Map Learning with STL-Based Conflict Resolution
summary: We address multi-robot motion planning under Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications with kinodynamic constraints. Exact approaches face scalability bottlenecks and limited adaptability, while conventional sampling-based methods require excessive samples to construct optimal trajectories. We propose a two-stage framework integrating sampling-based online learning with formal STL reasoning. At the single-robot level, our constrained Bayesian Optimization-based Tree search (cBOT) planner uses a Gaussian process as a surrogate model to learn local cost maps and feasibility constraints, generating shorter collision-free trajectories with fewer samples. At the multi-robot level, our STL-enhanced Kinodynamic Conflict-Based Search (STL-KCBS) algorithm incorporates STL monitoring into conflict detection and resolution, ensuring specification satisfaction while maintaining scalability and probabilistic completeness. Benchmarking demonstrates improved trajectory efficiency and safety over existing methods. Real-world experiments with autonomous surface vehicles validate robustness and practical applicability in uncertain environments. The STLcBOT Planner will be released as an open-source package, and videos of real-world and simulated experiments are available at https://stlbot.github.io/.

AI.tldr: A two-stage framework combining constrained Bayesian Optimization-based Tree search (cBOT) for single-robot kinodynamic planning with STL-enhanced Kinodynamic Conflict-Based Search (STL-KCBS) for multi-robot coordination under Signal Temporal Logic specifications.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for multi-robot motion planning under STL specifications face scalability bottlenecks (exact methods) or require excessive samples (sampling-based methods), limiting their practical applicability in complex environments with kinodynamic constraints.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: 1) Single-robot level uses cBOT planner with Gaussian process surrogate model to learn local cost maps and feasibility constraints, generating collision-free trajectories with fewer samples. 2) Multi-robot level employs STL-KCBS algorithm that incorporates STL monitoring into conflict detection and resolution for specification satisfaction while maintaining scalability.
AI.result: Benchmarking shows improved trajectory efficiency and safety over existing methods. Real-world experiments with autonomous surface vehicles validate robustness and practical applicability in uncertain environments. The approach demonstrates probabilistic completeness while handling kinodynamic constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed STLcBOT framework effectively addresses multi-robot motion planning under STL specifications by integrating sampling-based online learning with formal STL reasoning, offering a scalable solution with open-source availability for practical deployment.

title: SAHOO: Safeguarded Alignment for High-Order Optimization Objectives in Recursive Self-Improvement
comment: Published at ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement. 20 pages, 5 figures
summary: Recursive self-improvement is moving from theory to practice: modern systems can critique, revise, and evaluate their own outputs, yet iterative self-modification risks subtle alignment drift. We introduce SAHOO, a practical framework to monitor and control drift through three safeguards: (i) the Goal Drift Index (GDI), a learned multi-signal detector combining semantic, lexical, structural, and distributional measures; (ii) constraint preservation checks that enforce safety-critical invariants such as syntactic correctness and non-hallucination; and (iii) regression-risk quantification to flag improvement cycles that undo prior gains. Across 189 tasks in code generation, mathematical reasoning, and truthfulness, SAHOO produces substantial quality gains, including 18.3 percent improvement in code tasks and 16.8 percent in reasoning, while preserving constraints in two domains and maintaining low violations in truthfulness. Thresholds are calibrated on a small validation set of 18 tasks across three cycles. We further map the capability-alignment frontier, showing efficient early improvement cycles but rising alignment costs later and exposing domain-specific tensions such as fluency versus factuality. SAHOO therefore makes alignment preservation during recursive self-improvement measurable, deployable, and systematically validated at scale.

AI.tldr: SAHOO is a framework for monitoring and controlling alignment drift during recursive self-improvement of AI systems, using multi-signal detection, constraint preservation, and regression-risk quantification to enable measurable alignment preservation.
AI.motivation: As recursive self-improvement moves from theory to practice, iterative self-modification risks subtle alignment drift where systems may gradually deviate from their intended goals and constraints while improving capabilities.
AI.method: SAHOO employs three safeguards: (1) Goal Drift Index (GDI) - a learned multi-signal detector combining semantic, lexical, structural, and distributional measures; (2) constraint preservation checks that enforce safety-critical invariants; and (3) regression-risk quantification to flag improvement cycles that undo prior gains.
AI.result: Across 189 tasks in code generation, mathematical reasoning, and truthfulness, SAHOO produces substantial quality gains (18.3% improvement in code tasks, 16.8% in reasoning) while preserving constraints in two domains and maintaining low violations in truthfulness. Thresholds were calibrated on 18 validation tasks across three cycles.
AI.conclusion: SAHOO makes alignment preservation during recursive self-improvement measurable, deployable, and systematically validated at scale, revealing domain-specific tensions (e.g., fluency vs. factuality) and showing that early improvement cycles are efficient but alignment costs rise later.

title: Task-Level Decisions to Gait Level Control: A Hierarchical Policy Approach for Quadruped Navigation
summary: Real-world quadruped navigation is constrained by a scale mismatch between high-level navigation decisions and low-level gait execution, as well as by instabilities under out-of-distribution environmental changes. Such variations challenge sim-to-real transfer and can trigger falls when policies lack explicit interfaces for adaptation. In this paper, we present a hierarchical policy architecture for quadrupedal navigation, termed Task-level Decision to Gait Control (TDGC). A low-level policy, trained with reinforcement learning in simulation, delivers gait-conditioned locomotion and maps task requirements to a compact set of controllable behavior parameters, enabling robust mode generation and smooth switching. A high-level policy makes task-centric decisions from sparse semantic or geometric terrain cues and translates them into low-level targets, forming a traceable decision pipeline without dense maps or high-resolution terrain reconstruction. Different from end-to-end approaches, our architecture provides explicit interfaces for deployment-time tuning, fault diagnosis, and policy refinement. We introduce a structured curriculum with performance-driven progression that expands environmental difficulty and disturbance ranges. Experiments show higher task success rates on mixed terrains and out-of-distribution tests.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical quadruped navigation architecture (TDGC) separates high-level task decisions from low-level gait control, enabling robust sim-to-real transfer and explicit adaptation interfaces.
AI.motivation: Addresses scale mismatch between navigation decisions and gait execution, and instability under out-of-distribution environmental changes that challenge sim-to-real transfer and cause falls in end-to-end approaches.
AI.method: Two-level hierarchical policy: low-level RL-trained gait controller maps task requirements to behavior parameters; high-level policy makes task decisions from sparse terrain cues and translates them to low-level targets. Uses structured curriculum with performance-driven progression.
AI.result: Higher task success rates on mixed terrains and out-of-distribution tests compared to end-to-end approaches.
AI.conclusion: TDGC architecture provides explicit interfaces for deployment tuning, fault diagnosis, and policy refinement, enabling robust quadruped navigation without dense maps or high-resolution terrain reconstruction.

title: Talk Freely, Execute Strictly: Schema-Gated Agentic AI for Flexible and Reproducible Scientific Workflows
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can now translate a researcher's plain-language goal into executable computation, yet scientific workflows demand determinism, provenance, and governance that are difficult to guarantee when an LLM decides what runs. Semi-structured interviews with 18 experts across 10 industrial R&D stakeholders surface 2 competing requirements--deterministic, constrained execution and conversational flexibility without workflow rigidity--together with boundary properties (human-in-the-loop control and transparency) that any resolution must satisfy. We propose schema-gated orchestration as the resolving principle: the schema becomes a mandatory execution boundary at the composed-workflow level, so that nothing runs unless the complete action--including cross-step dependencies--validates against a machine-checkable specification.
  We operationalize the 2 requirements as execution determinism (ED) and conversational flexibility (CF), and use these axes to review 20 systems spanning 5 architectural groups along a validation-scope spectrum. Scores are assigned via a multi-model protocol--15 independent sessions across 3 LLM families--yielding substantial-to-near-perfect inter-model agreement (Krippendorff a=0.80 for ED and a=0.98 for CF), demonstrating that multi-model LLM scoring can serve as a reusable alternative to human expert panels for architectural assessment.
  The resulting landscape reveals an empirical Pareto front--no reviewed system achieves both high flexibility and high determinism--but a convergence zone emerges between the generative and workflow-centric extremes. We argue that a schema-gated architecture, separating conversational from execution authority, is positioned to decouple this trade-off, and distill 3 operational principles--clarification-before-execution, constrained plan-act orchestration, and tool-to-workflow-level gating--to guide adoption.

AI.tldr: Schema-gated orchestration resolves the tension between deterministic execution and conversational flexibility in LLM-driven scientific workflows by using machine-checkable schemas as mandatory execution boundaries.
AI.motivation: LLMs can translate plain-language goals into executable computation, but scientific workflows require determinism, provenance, and governance that are difficult to guarantee when LLMs autonomously decide what runs. Interviews with industrial R&D experts revealed competing requirements: deterministic constrained execution vs. conversational flexibility without workflow rigidity.
AI.method: Proposed schema-gated orchestration where schemas become mandatory execution boundaries at the composed-workflow level. Operationalized requirements as execution determinism (ED) and conversational flexibility (CF). Reviewed 20 systems across 5 architectural groups using multi-model LLM scoring protocol (15 sessions across 3 LLM families) with inter-model agreement validation.
AI.result: Multi-model LLM scoring showed substantial-to-near-perfect inter-model agreement (Krippendorff α=0.80 for ED, α=0.98 for CF). Landscape revealed empirical Pareto front - no system achieves both high flexibility and high determinism. Identified convergence zone between generative and workflow-centric extremes.
AI.conclusion: Schema-gated architecture separating conversational from execution authority can decouple the flexibility-determinism trade-off. Three operational principles distilled: clarification-before-execution, constrained plan-act orchestration, and tool-to-workflow-level gating to guide adoption.

title: CDF-Glove: A Cable-Driven Force Feedback Glove for Dexterous Teleoperation
summary: High-quality teleoperated demonstrations are a primary bottleneck for imitation learning (IL) in dexterous manipulation. However, haptic feedback provides operators with real-time contact information, enabling real-time finger posture adjustments, and thereby improving demonstration quality. Existing dexterous teleoperation platforms typically omit haptic feedback and remain bulky and expensive. We introduce CDF-Glove, a lightweight and low cost cable-driven force-feedback glove. The real-time state is available for 20 finger degrees of freedom (DoF), of which 16 are directly sensed and 4 are passively coupled (inferred from kinematic constraints). We develop a kinematic model and control stack for the glove, and validate them across multiple robotic hands with diverse kinematics and DoF. The CDF-Glove achieves distal joint repeatability of 0.4 degrees, and delivers about 200 ms force feedback latency, yielding a 4x improvement in task success rate relative to no-feedback teleoperation. We collect two bimanual teleoperation datasets, on which we train and evaluate Diffusion Policy baselines. Compared to kinesthetic teaching, the policies trained in our teleoperated demonstrations increase the average success rate by 55% and reduce the mean completion time by approximately 15.2 seconds (a 47.2% relative reduction). In particular, the CDF-Glove costs approximately US$230. The code and designs are released as open source at https://cdfglove.github.io/.

AI.tldr: CDF-Glove: A lightweight, low-cost cable-driven force-feedback glove for dexterous teleoperation that improves demonstration quality for imitation learning, achieving 4x task success rate improvement over no-feedback teleoperation.
AI.motivation: High-quality teleoperated demonstrations are a bottleneck for imitation learning in dexterous manipulation. Existing teleoperation platforms typically omit haptic feedback, are bulky, expensive, and lack real-time contact information needed for precise finger posture adjustments.
AI.method: Developed CDF-Glove, a lightweight, low-cost cable-driven force-feedback glove with 20 finger DoF sensing (16 direct, 4 inferred). Created kinematic model and control stack validated across multiple robotic hands with diverse kinematics. Collected bimanual teleoperation datasets and trained Diffusion Policy baselines.
AI.result: Achieved 0.4° distal joint repeatability, ~200ms force feedback latency, 4x task success rate improvement over no-feedback teleoperation. Policies trained on teleoperated demonstrations increased average success rate by 55% and reduced mean completion time by ~15.2 seconds (47.2% reduction) compared to kinesthetic teaching. Cost: ~US$230.
AI.conclusion: CDF-Glove provides an effective, affordable solution for high-quality dexterous teleoperation with haptic feedback, significantly improving demonstration quality for imitation learning while being lightweight, low-cost, and open-source.

title: Boosting deep Reinforcement Learning using pretraining with Logical Options
summary: Deep reinforcement learning agents are often misaligned, as they over-exploit early reward signals. Recently, several symbolic approaches have addressed these challenges by encoding sparse objectives along with aligned plans. However, purely symbolic architectures are complex to scale and difficult to apply to continuous settings. Hence, we propose a hybrid approach, inspired by humans' ability to acquire new skills. We use a two-stage framework that injects symbolic structure into neural-based reinforcement learning agents without sacrificing the expressivity of deep policies. Our method, called Hybrid Hierarchical RL (H^2RL), introduces a logical option-based pretraining strategy to steer the learning policy away from short-term reward loops and toward goal-directed behavior while allowing the final policy to be refined via standard environment interaction. Empirically, we show that this approach consistently improves long-horizon decision-making and yields agents that outperform strong neural, symbolic, and neuro-symbolic baselines.

AI.tldr: H²RL: Hybrid Hierarchical RL combines symbolic planning with neural RL to prevent reward over-exploitation and improve long-horizon decision-making.
AI.motivation: Deep RL agents often over-exploit early reward signals and become misaligned, while purely symbolic approaches are difficult to scale and apply to continuous settings. The paper aims to combine the strengths of both approaches.
AI.method: H²RL uses a two-stage hybrid framework with logical option-based pretraining to inject symbolic structure into neural RL agents. It steers learning away from short-term reward loops toward goal-directed behavior while maintaining deep policy expressivity.
AI.result: The approach consistently improves long-horizon decision-making and outperforms strong neural, symbolic, and neuro-symbolic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid hierarchical RL effectively addresses misalignment in deep RL by combining symbolic structure with neural learning, enabling better long-term planning while maintaining scalability and applicability to continuous domains.

title: Hierarchical Latent Action Model
comment: ICLR 2026 Workshop - 2nd Workshop on World Models: Understanding, Modelling and Scaling
summary: Latent Action Models (LAMs) enable learning from actionless data for applications ranging from robotic control to interactive world models. However, existing LAMs typically focus on short-horizon frame transitions and capture low-level motion while overlooking longer-term temporal structure. In contrast, actionless videos often contain temporally extended and high-level skills. We present HiLAM, a hierarchical latent action model that discovers latent skills by modeling long-term temporal information. To capture these dependencies across long horizons, we utilize a pretrained LAM as a low-level extractor. This architecture aggregates latent action sequences, which contain the underlying dynamic patterns of the video, into high-level latent skills. Our experiments demonstrate that HiLAM improves over the baseline and exhibits robust dynamic skill discovery.

AI.tldr: HiLAM is a hierarchical latent action model that discovers high-level latent skills from actionless videos by modeling long-term temporal information, improving over baseline LAMs that only capture short-horizon frame transitions.
AI.motivation: Existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) focus on short-horizon frame transitions and capture only low-level motion, overlooking longer-term temporal structure in actionless videos that often contain temporally extended and high-level skills.
AI.method: HiLAM uses a pretrained LAM as a low-level extractor to capture underlying dynamic patterns, then aggregates latent action sequences into high-level latent skills through hierarchical modeling of long-term temporal dependencies.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that HiLAM improves over the baseline and exhibits robust dynamic skill discovery from actionless video data.
AI.conclusion: HiLAM successfully addresses the limitation of existing LAMs by discovering high-level latent skills through hierarchical modeling of long-term temporal information in actionless videos.

title: OpenHEART: Opening Heterogeneous Articulated Objects with a Legged Manipulator
summary: Legged manipulators offer high mobility and versatile manipulation. However, robust interaction with heterogeneous articulated objects, such as doors, drawers, and cabinets, remains challenging because of the diverse articulation types of the objects and the complex dynamics of the legged robot. Existing reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches often rely on high-dimensional sensory inputs, leading to sample inefficiency. In this paper, we propose a robust and sample-efficient framework for opening heterogeneous articulated objects with a legged manipulator. In particular, we propose Sampling-based Abstracted Feature Extraction (SAFE), which encodes handle and panel geometry into a compact low-dimensional representation, improving cross-domain generalization. Additionally, Articulation Information Estimator (ArtIEst) is introduced to adaptively mix proprioception with exteroception to estimate opening direction and range of motion for each object. The proposed framework was deployed to manipulate various heterogeneous articulated objects in simulation and real-world robot systems. Videos can be found on the project website: https://openheart-icra.github.io/OpenHEART/

AI.tldr: A robust and sample-efficient reinforcement learning framework for legged manipulators to open heterogeneous articulated objects using compact feature extraction and adaptive sensor fusion.
AI.motivation: Legged manipulators struggle with robust interaction with diverse articulated objects (doors, drawers, cabinets) due to heterogeneous articulation types and complex robot dynamics, while existing RL approaches are sample-inefficient due to high-dimensional sensory inputs.
AI.method: Proposes Sampling-based Abstracted Feature Extraction (SAFE) to encode handle and panel geometry into compact low-dimensional representations, and Articulation Information Estimator (ArtIEst) to adaptively mix proprioception with exteroception for estimating opening direction and range of motion.
AI.result: The framework was successfully deployed to manipulate various heterogeneous articulated objects in both simulation and real-world robot systems, demonstrating improved cross-domain generalization and sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SAFE and ArtIEst components enable robust and sample-efficient manipulation of diverse articulated objects by legged manipulators, addressing key challenges in cross-domain generalization and sensor fusion for complex manipulation tasks.

title: Terrain characterization and locomotion adaptation in a small-scale lizard-inspired robot
summary: Unlike their large-scale counterparts, small-scale robots are largely confined to laboratory environments and are rarely deployed in real-world settings. As robot size decreases, robot-terrain interactions fundamentally change; however, there remains a lack of systematic understanding of what sensory information small-scale robots should acquire and how they should respond when traversing complex natural terrains. To address these challenges, we develop a Small-scale, Intelligent, Lizard-inspired, Adaptive Robot (SILA Bot) capable of adapting to diverse substrates. We use granular media of varying depths as a controlled yet representative terrain paradigm. We show that the optimal body movement pattern (ranging from standing-wave bending that assists limb retraction on flat ground to traveling-wave undulation that generates thrust in deep granular media) can be parameterized and approximated as a linear function of granular depth. Furthermore, proprioceptive signals, such as joint torque, provide sufficient information to estimate granular depth via a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier, achieving 95% accuracy. Leveraging these relationships, we design a simple linear feedback controller that modulates body phase and substantially improves locomotion performance on terrains with unknown depth. Together, these results establish a principled framework for perception and control in small-scale locomotion and enable effective terrain-adaptive locomotion while maintaining low computational complexity.

AI.tldr: Small-scale robots struggle with real-world terrain adaptation; SILA Bot uses lizard-inspired design and proprioceptive sensing to achieve terrain-adaptive locomotion via linear feedback control based on granular depth estimation.
AI.motivation: Small-scale robots are confined to labs due to inadequate understanding of robot-terrain interactions at small scales. There's a need for systematic approaches to sensory acquisition and adaptive responses for traversing complex natural terrains.
AI.method: Developed SILA Bot (Small-scale, Intelligent, Lizard-inspired, Adaptive Robot) with granular media as controlled terrain paradigm. Used proprioceptive signals (joint torque) with K-Nearest Neighbors classifier to estimate granular depth, then designed linear feedback controller to modulate body phase based on depth.
AI.result: Optimal body movement patterns (standing-wave to traveling-wave undulation) can be parameterized as linear function of granular depth. Depth estimation achieved 95% accuracy via KNN classifier. Linear feedback controller substantially improved locomotion performance on unknown-depth terrains.
AI.conclusion: Established principled framework for perception and control in small-scale locomotion, enabling effective terrain-adaptive locomotion with low computational complexity through proprioceptive sensing and simple linear control.

title: Expert Knowledge-driven Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Racing via Trajectory Guidance and Dynamics Constraints
summary: Reinforcement learning has demonstrated significant potential in the field of autonomous driving. However, it suffers from defects such as training instability and unsafe action outputs when faced with autonomous racing environments characterized by high dynamics and strong nonlinearities. To this end, this paper proposes a trajectory guidance and dynamics constraints Reinforcement Learning (TraD-RL) method for autonomous racing. The key features of this method are as follows: 1) leveraging the prior expert racing line to construct an augmented state representation and facilitate reward shaping, thereby integrating domain knowledge to stabilize early-stage policy learning; 2) embedding explicit vehicle dynamic priors into a safe operating envelope formulated via control barrier functions to enable safety-constrained learning; and 3) adopting a multi-stage curriculum learning strategy that shifts from expert-guided learning to autonomous exploration, allowing the learned policy to surpass expert-level performance. The proposed method is evaluated in a high-fidelity simulation environment modeled after the Tempelhof Airport Street Circuit. Experimental results demonstrate that TraD-RL effectively improves both lap speed and driving stability of the autonomous racing vehicle, achieving a synergistic optimization of racing performance and safety.

AI.tldr: TraD-RL: A reinforcement learning method for autonomous racing that combines expert trajectory guidance, vehicle dynamics constraints via control barrier functions, and multi-stage curriculum learning to improve both racing performance and safety.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement learning suffers from training instability and unsafe action outputs in high-dynamics autonomous racing environments with strong nonlinearities, necessitating methods that can ensure both performance and safety.
AI.method: 1) Uses prior expert racing line for augmented state representation and reward shaping to stabilize early learning; 2) Embeds vehicle dynamics priors via control barrier functions to create safe operating envelope; 3) Implements multi-stage curriculum learning transitioning from expert guidance to autonomous exploration.
AI.result: Evaluation in high-fidelity Tempelhof Airport Street Circuit simulation shows TraD-RL effectively improves both lap speed and driving stability, achieving synergistic optimization of racing performance and safety.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TraD-RL method successfully addresses RL limitations in autonomous racing by integrating domain knowledge, safety constraints, and progressive learning strategies to achieve expert-surpassing performance with enhanced stability.

title: TADPO: Reinforcement Learning Goes Off-road
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at ICRA 2026
summary: Off-road autonomous driving poses significant challenges such as navigating unmapped, variable terrain with uncertain and diverse dynamics. Addressing these challenges requires effective long-horizon planning and adaptable control. Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a promising solution by learning control policies directly from interaction. However, because off-road driving is a long-horizon task with low-signal rewards, standard RL methods are challenging to apply in this setting. We introduce TADPO, a novel policy gradient formulation that extends Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), leveraging off-policy trajectories for teacher guidance and on-policy trajectories for student exploration. Building on this, we develop a vision-based, end-to-end RL system for high-speed off-road driving, capable of navigating extreme slopes and obstacle-rich terrain. We demonstrate our performance in simulation and, importantly, zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a full-scale off-road vehicle. To our knowledge, this work represents the first deployment of RL-based policies on a full-scale off-road platform.

AI.tldr: TADPO: A novel RL policy gradient method combining off-policy teacher guidance and on-policy student exploration for vision-based end-to-end off-road autonomous driving, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on full-scale vehicles.
AI.motivation: Off-road autonomous driving faces challenges with unmapped, variable terrain and uncertain dynamics requiring long-horizon planning and adaptable control. Standard RL methods struggle due to long-horizon tasks with low-signal rewards in this setting.
AI.method: TADPO (novel policy gradient formulation extending PPO) leverages off-policy trajectories for teacher guidance and on-policy trajectories for student exploration. Developed a vision-based, end-to-end RL system for high-speed off-road driving capable of navigating extreme slopes and obstacle-rich terrain.
AI.result: Demonstrated performance in simulation and achieved zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a full-scale off-road vehicle. Represents the first deployment of RL-based policies on a full-scale off-road platform.
AI.conclusion: TADPO successfully addresses off-road driving challenges by combining teacher-student learning in RL, enabling effective vision-based autonomous navigation with real-world deployment on full-scale vehicles through sim-to-real transfer.

title: DexEMG: Towards Dexterous Teleoperation System via EMG2Pose Generalization
summary: High-fidelity teleoperation of dexterous robotic hands is essential for bringing robots into unstructured domestic environments. However, existing teleoperation systems often face a trade-off between performance and portability: vision-based capture systems are constrained by costs and line-of-sight requirements, while mechanical exoskeletons are bulky and physically restrictive. In this paper, we present DexEMG, a lightweight and cost-effective teleoperation system leveraging surface electromyography (sEMG) to bridge the gap between human intent and robotic execution. We first collect a synchronized dataset of sEMG signals and hand poses via a MoCap glove to train EMG2Pose, a neural network capable of continuously predicting hand kinematics directly from muscle activity. To ensure seamless control, we develop a robust hand retargeting algorithm that maps the predicted poses onto a multi-fingered dexterous hand in real-time. Experimental results demonstrate that DexEMG achieves high precision in diverse teleoperation tasks. Notably, our system exhibits strong generalization capabilities across novel objects and complex environments without the need for intensive individual-specific recalibration. This work offers a scalable and intuitive interface for both general-purpose robotic manipulation and assistive technologies.

AI.tldr: DexEMG: A lightweight teleoperation system using surface EMG signals to predict hand kinematics for dexterous robotic control, achieving high precision without intensive recalibration.
AI.motivation: Existing teleoperation systems face trade-offs between performance and portability - vision-based systems have cost/line-of-sight constraints, while mechanical exoskeletons are bulky and restrictive. There's a need for scalable, intuitive interfaces for robotic manipulation in unstructured environments.
AI.method: 1) Collect synchronized sEMG signals and hand poses using MoCap glove; 2) Train EMG2Pose neural network to predict hand kinematics from muscle activity; 3) Develop robust hand retargeting algorithm to map predicted poses onto multi-fingered dexterous hand in real-time.
AI.result: DexEMG achieves high precision in diverse teleoperation tasks, exhibits strong generalization across novel objects and complex environments, and requires minimal individual-specific recalibration.
AI.conclusion: DexEMG provides a scalable, cost-effective, and intuitive teleoperation interface suitable for both general-purpose robotic manipulation and assistive technologies, bridging the gap between human intent and robotic execution.

title: Restoring Linguistic Grounding in VLA Models via Train-Free Attention Recalibration
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable robots to perform manipulation tasks directly from natural language instructions and are increasingly viewed as a foundation for generalist robotic policies. However, their reliability under Out-of-Distribution (OOD) instructions remains underexplored. In this paper, we reveal a critical failure mode in which VLA policies continue executing visually plausible actions even when the language instruction contradicts the scene. We refer to this phenomenon as linguistic blindness, where VLA policies prioritize visual priors over instruction semantics during action generation. To systematically analyze this issue, we introduce ICBench, a diagnostic benchmark constructed from the LIBERO dataset that probes language-action coupling by injecting controlled OOD instruction contradictions while keeping the visual environment unchanged. Evaluations on three representative VLA architectures, including Pi0, Pi0.5 and OpenVLA OFT, show that these models frequently succeed at tasks despite logically impossible instructions, revealing a strong visual bias in action generation. To mitigate this issue, we propose Instruction-Guided Attention Recalibration (IGAR), a train-free inference-time mechanism that rebalances attention distributions to restore the influence of language instructions. IGAR operates without retraining or architectural modification and can be directly applied to existing VLA models. Experiments across 30 LIBERO tasks demonstrate that IGAR substantially reduces erroneous execution under OOD contradictory instructions while preserving baseline task performance. We additionally validate the approach on a real Franka robotic arm, where IGAR effectively prevents manipulation triggered by inconsistent instructions.

AI.tldr: VLA models suffer from "linguistic blindness" - they execute visually plausible actions even when instructions contradict the scene. The paper introduces ICBench to diagnose this issue and proposes IGAR, a train-free inference-time mechanism to recalibrate attention toward language instructions.
AI.motivation: VLA models are becoming foundation models for robotic policies but their reliability under Out-of-Distribution (OOD) instructions is underexplored. The paper identifies a critical failure mode where VLA policies prioritize visual priors over instruction semantics, executing actions even when instructions logically contradict the scene.
AI.method: 1) Introduce ICBench diagnostic benchmark constructed from LIBERO dataset to probe language-action coupling with controlled OOD instruction contradictions. 2) Propose Instruction-Guided Attention Recalibration (IGAR), a train-free inference-time mechanism that rebalances attention distributions to restore language instruction influence without retraining or architectural modifications.
AI.result: Evaluations on three VLA architectures (Pi0, Pi0.5, OpenVLA OFT) show models frequently succeed at tasks despite logically impossible instructions, revealing strong visual bias. IGAR substantially reduces erroneous execution under OOD contradictory instructions while preserving baseline task performance across 30 LIBERO tasks. Real-world validation on Franka robotic arm shows IGAR effectively prevents manipulation triggered by inconsistent instructions.
AI.conclusion: VLA models exhibit linguistic blindness where visual priors dominate instruction semantics. IGAR provides an effective, practical solution to mitigate this issue without model retraining, enhancing safety and reliability of VLA policies in real-world robotic applications.

title: AnyCamVLA: Zero-Shot Camera Adaptation for Viewpoint Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Despite remarkable progress in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) for robot manipulation, these large pre-trained models require fine-tuning to be deployed in specific environments. These fine-tuned models are highly sensitive to camera viewpoint changes that frequently occur in unstructured environments. In this paper, we propose a zero-shot camera adaptation framework without additional demonstration data, policy fine-tuning, or architectural modification. Our key idea is to virtually adjust test-time camera observations to match the training camera configuration in real-time. For that, we use a recent feed-forward novel view synthesis model which outputs high-quality target view images, handling both extrinsic and intrinsic parameters. This plug-and-play approach preserves the pre-trained capabilities of VLAs and applies to any RGB-based policy. Through extensive experiments on the LIBERO benchmark, our method consistently outperforms baselines that use data augmentation for policy fine-tuning or additional 3D-aware features for visual input. We further validate that our approach constantly enhances viewpoint robustness in real-world robotic manipulation scenarios, including settings with varying camera extrinsics, intrinsics, and freely moving handheld cameras.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot camera adaptation framework for vision-language-action models that virtually adjusts test-time camera observations to match training configurations without additional data or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action models for robot manipulation require fine-tuning for specific environments and are highly sensitive to camera viewpoint changes in unstructured settings, necessitating a robust adaptation method.
AI.method: Proposes a plug-and-play framework using feed-forward novel view synthesis to virtually adjust test-time camera observations in real-time, matching training camera configurations without policy modification or additional data.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines using data augmentation or 3D-aware features on LIBERO benchmark, and demonstrates enhanced viewpoint robustness in real-world robotic manipulation with varying camera parameters.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot camera adaptation via novel view synthesis effectively preserves pre-trained VLA capabilities while improving viewpoint robustness across diverse camera configurations without requiring additional training data or architectural changes.

title: Lifelong Embodied Navigation Learning
summary: Embodied navigation agents powered by large language models have shown strong performance on individual tasks but struggle to continually acquire new navigation skills, which suffer from catastrophic forgetting. We formalize this challenge as lifelong embodied navigation learning (LENL), where an agent is required to adapt to a sequence of navigation tasks spanning multiple scenes and diverse user instruction styles, while retaining previously learned knowledge. To tackle this problem, we propose Uni-Walker, a lifelong embodied navigation framework that decouples navigation knowledge into task-shared and task-specific components with Decoder Extension LoRA (DE-LoRA). To learn the shared knowledge, we design a knowledge inheritance strategy and an experts co-activation strategy to facilitate shared knowledge transfer and refinement across multiple navigation tasks. To learn the specific knowledge, we propose an expert subspace orthogonality constraint together and a navigation-specific chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to capture specific knowledge and enhance instruction-style understanding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of Uni-Walker for building universal navigation agents with lifelong learning.

AI.tldr: Uni-Walker is a lifelong embodied navigation framework that addresses catastrophic forgetting in LLM-powered navigation agents by decoupling knowledge into task-shared and task-specific components using Decoder Extension LoRA (DE-LoRA).
AI.motivation: Current embodied navigation agents powered by large language models perform well on individual tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting when required to continually acquire new navigation skills, limiting their ability to adapt to sequences of diverse navigation tasks.
AI.method: The framework decouples navigation knowledge into task-shared and task-specific components using DE-LoRA. For shared knowledge: knowledge inheritance strategy and experts co-activation strategy facilitate transfer and refinement. For specific knowledge: expert subspace orthogonality constraint and navigation-specific chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism capture specific knowledge and enhance instruction-style understanding.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of Uni-Walker for building universal navigation agents with lifelong learning capabilities, effectively addressing the catastrophic forgetting problem in lifelong embodied navigation learning.
AI.conclusion: Uni-Walker successfully tackles the lifelong embodied navigation learning challenge by decoupling knowledge components and implementing specialized strategies for both shared and specific knowledge acquisition, enabling agents to adapt to sequential navigation tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge.

title: Improved hopping control on slopes for small robots using spring mass modeling
summary: Hopping robots often lose balance on slopes because the tilted ground creates unwanted rotation at landing. This work analyzes that effect using a simple spring mass model and identifies how slope induced impulses destabilize the robot. To address this, we introduce two straightforward fixes, adjusting the bodys touchdown angle based on the slope and applying a small corrective torque before takeoff. Together, these steps effectively cancel the unwanted rotation caused by inclined terrain, allowing the robot to land smoothly and maintain stable hopping even on steep slopes. Moreover, the proposed method remains simple enough to implement on low cost robotic platforms without requiring complex sensing or computation. By combining this analytical model with minimal control actions, this approach provides a practical path toward reliable hopping on uneven terrain. The results from simulation confirm that even small slope aware adjustments can dramatically improve landing stability, making the technique suitable for future autonomous field robots that must navigate natural environments such as hills, rubble, and irregular outdoor landscapes.

AI.tldr: Simple spring-mass model reveals slope-induced rotation destabilizes hopping robots; two fixes (slope-adjusted touchdown angle + pre-takeoff corrective torque) cancel unwanted rotation for stable hopping on steep slopes.
AI.motivation: Hopping robots lose balance on slopes because tilted ground creates unwanted rotation at landing, destabilizing the robot on uneven terrain.
AI.method: Analyze slope effect using simple spring-mass model; introduce two fixes: adjust body's touchdown angle based on slope, and apply small corrective torque before takeoff to cancel unwanted rotation.
AI.result: Simulation confirms small slope-aware adjustments dramatically improve landing stability; method enables stable hopping even on steep slopes.
AI.conclusion: Combining analytical model with minimal control actions provides practical path toward reliable hopping on uneven terrain, suitable for low-cost robotic platforms navigating natural environments.

title: A Hazard-Informed Data Pipeline for Robotics Physical Safety
comment: 4th International Conference on Automation and Mechatronics Engineering (ICAME 2026)
summary: This report presents a structured Robotics Physical Safety Framework based on explicit asset declaration, systematic vulnerability enumeration, and hazard-driven synthetic data generation. The approach bridges classical risk engineering with modern machine learning pipelines, enabling safety envelope learning grounded in a formalized hazard ontology. The key contribution of this framework is the alignment between classical safety engineering, digital twin simulation, synthetic data generation, and machine learning model training.

AI.tldr: A robotics safety framework combining asset declaration, vulnerability analysis, and synthetic data generation to bridge traditional risk engineering with ML safety learning.
AI.motivation: To address the gap between classical safety engineering approaches and modern machine learning pipelines in robotics, enabling systematic safety analysis and learning through formalized hazard modeling.
AI.method: Structured framework based on: 1) explicit asset declaration, 2) systematic vulnerability enumeration, 3) hazard-driven synthetic data generation, and 4) safety envelope learning grounded in formalized hazard ontology.
AI.result: Framework enables alignment between classical safety engineering, digital twin simulation, synthetic data generation, and machine learning model training for robotics physical safety.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges traditional risk engineering with modern ML pipelines, providing a systematic approach to robotics physical safety through formalized hazard modeling and synthetic data generation.

title: Iterative Convex Optimization with Control Barrier Functions for Obstacle Avoidance among Polytopes
summary: Obstacle avoidance of polytopic obstacles by polytopic robots is a challenging problem in optimization-based control and trajectory planning. Many existing methods rely on smooth geometric approximations, such as hyperspheres or ellipsoids, which allow differentiable distance expressions but distort the true geometry and restrict the feasible set. Other approaches integrate exact polytope distances into nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), resulting in nonconvex programs that limit real-time performance. In this paper, we construct linear discrete-time control barrier function (DCBF) constraints by deriving supporting hyperplanes from exact closest-point computations between convex polytopes. We then propose a novel iterative convex MPC-DCBF framework, where local linearization of system dynamics and robot geometry ensures convexity of the finite-horizon optimization at each iteration. The resulting formulation reduces computational complexity and enables fast online implementation for safety-critical control and trajectory planning of general nonlinear dynamics. The framework extends to multi-robot and three-dimensional environments. Numerical experiments demonstrate collision-free navigation in cluttered maze scenarios with millisecond-level solve times.

AI.tldr: A novel iterative convex MPC-DCBF framework for polytopic obstacle avoidance using exact closest-point computations and local linearization to enable fast, collision-free navigation with millisecond solve times.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for polytopic obstacle avoidance either use smooth geometric approximations that distort true geometry and restrict feasible sets, or integrate exact polytope distances into nonlinear MPC resulting in nonconvex programs with poor real-time performance.
AI.method: Construct linear discrete-time control barrier function (DCBF) constraints by deriving supporting hyperplanes from exact closest-point computations between convex polytopes. Propose an iterative convex MPC-DCBF framework with local linearization of system dynamics and robot geometry to ensure convexity of finite-horizon optimization at each iteration.
AI.result: The framework reduces computational complexity and enables fast online implementation for safety-critical control and trajectory planning of general nonlinear dynamics. Numerical experiments demonstrate collision-free navigation in cluttered maze scenarios with millisecond-level solve times.
AI.conclusion: The proposed iterative convex MPC-DCBF framework effectively addresses the challenge of polytopic obstacle avoidance by combining exact geometry with convex optimization, enabling real-time performance while maintaining safety guarantees for complex nonlinear systems.

title: Fly360: Omnidirectional Obstacle Avoidance within Drone View
summary: Obstacle avoidance in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), as a fundamental capability, has gained increasing attention with the growing focus on spatial intelligence. However, current obstacle-avoidance methods mainly depend on limited field-of-view sensors and are ill-suited for UAV scenarios which require full-spatial awareness when the movement direction differs from the UAV's heading. This limitation motivates us to explore omnidirectional obstacle avoidance for panoramic drones with full-view perception. We first study an under explored problem setting in which a UAV must generate collision-free motion in environments with obstacles from arbitrary directions, and then construct a benchmark that consists of three representative flight tasks. Based on such settings, we propose Fly360, a two-stage perception-decision pipeline with a fixed random-yaw training strategy. At the perception stage, panoramic RGB observations are input and converted into depth maps as a robust intermediate representation. For the policy network, it is lightweight and used to output body-frame velocity commands from depth inputs. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Fly360 achieves stable omnidirectional obstacle avoidance and outperforms forward-view baselines across all tasks. Our model is available at https://zxkai.github.io/fly360/

AI.tldr: Fly360 enables omnidirectional obstacle avoidance for panoramic drones using a two-stage perception-decision pipeline with depth-based intermediate representation and lightweight policy network.
AI.motivation: Current UAV obstacle avoidance methods rely on limited field-of-view sensors and are unsuitable for scenarios requiring full-spatial awareness when movement direction differs from UAV heading, motivating exploration of omnidirectional obstacle avoidance for panoramic drones.
AI.method: Two-stage perception-decision pipeline: 1) Perception stage converts panoramic RGB observations into depth maps as robust intermediate representation, 2) Lightweight policy network outputs body-frame velocity commands from depth inputs using fixed random-yaw training strategy.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate stable omnidirectional obstacle avoidance, outperforming forward-view baselines across all three representative flight tasks in the constructed benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Fly360 successfully addresses the under-explored problem of omnidirectional obstacle avoidance for panoramic drones, providing a practical solution that achieves superior performance compared to conventional forward-view approaches.

title: Swooper: Learning High-Speed Aerial Grasping With a Simple Gripper
summary:
High-speed aerial grasping presents significant challenges due to the high demands on precise, responsive flight control and coordinated gripper manipulation. In this work, we propose Swooper, a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) based approach that achieves both precise flight control and active gripper control using a single lightweight neural network policy. Training such a policy directly via DRL is nontrivial due to the complexity of coordinating flight and grasping. To address this, we adopt a two-stage learning strategy: we first pre-train a flight control policy, and then fine-tune it to acquire grasping skills. With the carefully designed reward functions and training framework, the entire training process completes in under 60 minutes on a standard desktop with an Nvidia RTX 3060 GPU. To validate the trained policy in the real world, we develop a lightweight quadrotor grasping platform equipped with a simple off-the-shelf gripper, and deploy the policy in a zero-shot manner on the onboard Raspberry Pi 4B computer, where each inference takes only about 1.0 ms. In 25 real-world trials, our policy achieves an 84% grasp success rate and grasping speeds of up to 1.5 m/s without any fine-tuning. This matches the robustness and agility of state-of-the-art classical systems with sophisticated grippers, highlighting the capability of DRL for learning a robust control policy that seamlessly integrates high-speed flight and grasping. The supplementary video is available for more results.
  Video: https://zikenhuang.github.io/Swooper/.

AI.tldr: Swooper: A DRL-based approach for high-speed aerial grasping using a single lightweight neural network policy trained in under 60 minutes, achieving 84% success rate at speeds up to 1.5 m/s with zero-shot real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: High-speed aerial grasping requires precise flight control coordinated with gripper manipulation, which is challenging to achieve with conventional methods. The paper aims to develop a lightweight, efficient solution using deep reinforcement learning that can handle both flight and grasping in a unified manner.
AI.method: A two-stage DRL training approach: first pre-train a flight control policy, then fine-tune it to acquire grasping skills. Uses carefully designed reward functions and training framework. The lightweight policy is deployed zero-shot on Raspberry Pi 4B with 1.0 ms inference time.
AI.result: Training completes in under 60 minutes on RTX 3060 GPU. Real-world deployment achieves 84% grasp success rate in 25 trials at speeds up to 1.5 m/s without fine-tuning. Matches state-of-the-art classical systems with sophisticated grippers.
AI.conclusion: DRL can learn robust control policies that seamlessly integrate high-speed flight and grasping, achieving performance comparable to sophisticated classical systems with simple off-the-shelf hardware and efficient training.

title: How to Model Your Crazyflie Brushless
summary: The Crazyflie quadcopter is widely recognized as a leading platform for nano-quadcopter research. In early 2025, the Crazyflie Brushless was introduced, featuring brushless motors that provide around 50% more thrust compared to the brushed motors of its predecessor, the Crazyflie 2.1. This advancement has opened new opportunities for research in agile nano-quadcopter control. To support researchers utilizing this new platform, this work presents a dynamics model of the Crazyflie Brushless and identifies its key parameters. Through simulations and hardware analyses, we assess the accuracy of our model. We furthermore demonstrate its suitability for reinforcement learning applications by training an end-to-end neural network position controller and learning a backflip controller capable of executing two complete rotations with a vertical movement of just 1.8 meters. This showcases the model's ability to facilitate the learning of controllers and acrobatic maneuvers that successfully transfer from simulation to hardware. Utilizing this application, we investigate the impact of domain randomization on control performance, offering valuable insights into bridging the sim-to-real gap with the presented model. We have open-sourced the entire project, enabling users of the Crazyflie Brushless to swiftly implement and test their own controllers on an accurate simulation platform.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a dynamics model for the Crazyflie Brushless quadcopter, validates it through simulation and hardware, demonstrates its utility for reinforcement learning (including position control and backflip maneuvers), and investigates domain randomization for sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: The Crazyflie Brushless platform offers improved thrust capabilities over its predecessor, creating new research opportunities in agile nano-quadcopter control. However, there's a need for an accurate dynamics model to support researchers in developing and testing controllers, particularly for reinforcement learning applications.
AI.method: Developed a dynamics model of the Crazyflie Brushless and identified key parameters. Validated model accuracy through simulations and hardware analyses. Demonstrated model utility by training an end-to-end neural network position controller and learning a backflip controller capable of two complete rotations. Investigated domain randomization effects on control performance for sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: Successfully created and validated an accurate dynamics model. Demonstrated the model's effectiveness for reinforcement learning by achieving successful position control and executing a backflip maneuver with two complete rotations using only 1.8 meters of vertical movement. Showed that the model facilitates learning controllers that successfully transfer from simulation to hardware.
AI.conclusion: The presented dynamics model for the Crazyflie Brushless provides an accurate simulation platform for researchers. It successfully enables reinforcement learning applications and facilitates sim-to-real transfer, with domain randomization offering valuable insights for bridging the reality gap. The open-sourced project allows rapid implementation and testing of custom controllers.

title: PROBE: Probabilistic Occupancy BEV Encoding with Analytical Translation Robustness for 3D Place Recognition
summary: We present PROBE (PRobabilistic Occupancy BEV Encoding), a learning-free LiDAR place recognition descriptor that models each BEV cell's occupancy as a Bernoulli random variable. Rather than relying on discrete point-cloud perturbations, PROBE analytically marginalizes over continuous Cartesian translations via the polar Jacobian, yielding a distance-adaptive angular uncertainty $σ_θ= σ_t / r$ in $\mathcal{O}(R \times S)$ time. The primary parameter $σ_t$ represents the expected translational uncertainty in meters, a sensor-independent physical quantity allowing cross-sensor generalization without per-dataset tuning. Pairwise similarity combines a Bernoulli-KL Jaccard with exponential uncertainty gating and FFT-based height cosine similarity for rotation alignment. Evaluated on four datasets spanning four diverse LiDAR types, PROBE achieves the highest accuracy among handcrafted descriptors in multi-session evaluation and competitive single-session performance against both handcrafted and supervised baselines. The source code and supplementary materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/probe-pr.

AI.tldr: PROBE is a learning-free LiDAR place recognition descriptor that models BEV cell occupancy as Bernoulli random variables, analytically marginalizes over continuous translations via polar Jacobian, and achieves competitive performance across diverse LiDAR sensors without dataset-specific tuning.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for robust LiDAR place recognition that can generalize across different sensor types without requiring dataset-specific tuning or learning-based approaches. Existing methods often rely on discrete perturbations or require per-dataset optimization, limiting cross-sensor applicability.
AI.method: PROBE models each BEV cell's occupancy as a Bernoulli random variable and analytically marginalizes over continuous Cartesian translations using the polar Jacobian, yielding distance-adaptive angular uncertainty σ_θ = σ_t / r. The method uses a Bernoulli-KL Jaccard similarity with exponential uncertainty gating and FFT-based height cosine similarity for rotation alignment, operating in O(R × S) time.
AI.result: Evaluated on four datasets spanning four diverse LiDAR types, PROBE achieves the highest accuracy among handcrafted descriptors in multi-session evaluation and competitive single-session performance against both handcrafted and supervised baselines, demonstrating cross-sensor generalization without per-dataset tuning.
AI.conclusion: PROBE provides an effective, learning-free approach to LiDAR place recognition that generalizes across different sensor types through its physics-based parameterization (σ_t as expected translational uncertainty) and analytical marginalization over continuous translations, offering practical advantages for real-world deployment.

title: Proprioceptive Shape Estimation of Tensegrity Manipulators Using Energy Minimisation
summary: Shape estimation is fundamental for controlling continuously bending tensegrity manipulators, yet achieving it remains a challenge. Although using exteroceptive sensors makes the implementation straightforward, it is costly and limited to specific environments. Proprioceptive approaches, by contrast, do not suffer from these limitations. So far, several methods have been proposed; however, to our knowledge, there are no proven examples of large-scale tensegrity structures used as manipulators. This paper demonstrates that shape estimation of the entire tensegrity manipulator can be achieved using only the inclination angle information relative to gravity for each strut. Inclination angle information is intrinsic sensory data that can be obtained simply by attaching an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to each strut. Experiments conducted on a five-layer tensegrity manipulator with 20 struts and a total length of 1160 mm demonstrate that the proposed method can estimate the shape with an accuracy of 2.1 \% of the total manipulator length, from arbitrary initial conditions under both static conditions and maintains stable shape estimation under external disturbances.

AI.tldr: Shape estimation for tensegrity manipulators using only strut inclination angles from IMUs achieves 2.1% accuracy relative to total length.
AI.motivation: Shape estimation is crucial for controlling continuously bending tensegrity manipulators. Exteroceptive sensors are costly and environment-limited, while proprioceptive approaches avoid these issues but lack proven examples for large-scale tensegrity manipulators.
AI.method: Uses only inclination angle information relative to gravity for each strut, obtained via IMUs attached to struts. This intrinsic sensory data enables shape estimation of the entire tensegrity manipulator without external sensors.
AI.result: Experiments on a five-layer tensegrity manipulator with 20 struts (1160 mm total length) show shape estimation accuracy of 2.1% of total manipulator length. Works from arbitrary initial conditions under static conditions and maintains stable estimation under external disturbances.
AI.conclusion: Proprioceptive shape estimation using only strut inclination angles is feasible and effective for large-scale tensegrity manipulators, achieving high accuracy with simple IMU-based sensing.

title: HarvestFlex: Strawberry Harvesting via Vision-Language-Action Policy Adaptation in the Wild
summary: This work presents the first study on transferring vision-language-action (VLA) policies to real greenhouse tabletop strawberry harvesting, a long-horizon, unstructured task challenged by occlusion and specular reflections. We built an end-to-end closed-loop system on the HarvestFlex platform using three-view RGB sensing (two fixed scene views plus a wrist-mounted view) and intentionally avoided depth clouds and explicit geometric calibration. We collected 3.71 h of VR teleoperated demonstrations (227 episodes) and fine-tuned pi_0, pi_0.5, and WALL-OSS with full fine-tuning and LoRA. Under a unified 50 trials real-greenhouse protocol and metrics spanning completion, pi_0.5 with full fine-tuning achieved success rate of 74.0% with 32.6 s/pick and damage rate of 4.1%. Asynchronous inference-control decoupling further improved performance over synchronous deployment. Results showed non-trivial closed-loop picking with fewer than four hours of real data, while remaining limited by close-range observability loss and contact-dynamics mismatch. A demonstration video is available at: https://youtu.be/bN8ZowZKPMI.

AI.tldr: First study transferring vision-language-action policies to real greenhouse strawberry harvesting using end-to-end closed-loop system with three-view RGB sensing, achieving 74% success rate with under 4 hours of real data.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of transferring VLA policies to real-world long-horizon unstructured tasks like greenhouse strawberry harvesting, which is complicated by occlusion and specular reflections, while avoiding complex depth sensing and explicit calibration.
AI.method: Built end-to-end closed-loop system on HarvestFlex platform using three-view RGB sensing (two fixed scene views plus wrist-mounted view), collected 3.71 hours of VR teleoperated demonstrations (227 episodes), and fine-tuned pi_0, pi_0.5, and WALL-OSS models with both full fine-tuning and LoRA approaches.
AI.result: Under 50-trial real-greenhouse protocol, pi_0.5 with full fine-tuning achieved 74.0% success rate, 32.6 seconds per pick, and 4.1% damage rate. Asynchronous inference-control decoupling further improved performance over synchronous deployment.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrated non-trivial closed-loop picking with fewer than four hours of real data, showing feasibility of VLA policy transfer to complex real-world tasks, though limited by close-range observability loss and contact-dynamics mismatch.

title: MagRobot:An Open Simulator for Magnetically Navigated Robots
summary: Magnetic navigation systems, including magnetic tracking systems and magnetic actuation systems, have shown great potential for occlusion-free localization and remote control of intracorporeal medical devices and robots in minimally invasive medicine, such as capsule endoscopy and cardiovascular intervention. However, the design of magnetically navigated robots remains heavily reliant on experimental prototyping, which is time-consuming and costly. Furthermore, there is a lack of a consistent experimental environment to compare and benchmark the hardware and algorithms across different magnetic navigation systems. To address these challenges, we propose the first universal open-source simulation platform to facilitate research, design and benchmarking of magnetically navigated robots. Our simulator features an intuitive graphical user interface that enables the user to efficiently design, visualize, and analyze magnetic navigation systems for both rigid and soft robots. The proposed simulator is versatile, which can simulate both magnetic actuation and magnetic tracking tasks in diverse medical applications that involve deformable anatomies. The proposed simulator provides an open development environment, where the user can load third-party anatomical models and customize both hardware and algorithms of magnetic navigation systems. The fidelity of the simulator is validated using both phantom and ex vivo experiments of magnetic navigation of a continuum robot and a capsule robot with diverse magnetic actuation setups. Three use cases of the simulator, i.e., bronchoscopy, endovascular intervention, and gastrointestinal endoscopy, are implemented to demonstrate the functionality of the simulator. It is shown that the configuration and algorithms of magnetic navigation systems can be flexibly designed and optimized for better performance using the simulator.

AI.tldr: First universal open-source simulation platform for magnetically navigated robots in medical applications, enabling design, visualization, and benchmarking of magnetic navigation systems.
AI.motivation: Current design of magnetically navigated robots relies heavily on experimental prototyping (time-consuming, costly), and lacks consistent experimental environments for comparing hardware and algorithms across different magnetic navigation systems.
AI.method: Developed an intuitive graphical user interface simulator that can simulate both magnetic actuation and tracking tasks for rigid and soft robots in deformable anatomies. The platform allows loading third-party anatomical models and customizing hardware/algorithms, validated through phantom and ex vivo experiments with continuum and capsule robots.
AI.result: Simulator validated using phantom and ex vivo experiments with continuum and capsule robots across diverse magnetic actuation setups. Three use cases (bronchoscopy, endovascular intervention, gastrointestinal endoscopy) demonstrate functionality. Configuration and algorithms can be flexibly designed and optimized for better performance.
AI.conclusion: Proposed simulator addresses key challenges in magnetic navigation research by providing a universal open-source platform for design, visualization, and benchmarking, enabling more efficient development and optimization of magnetically navigated medical robots.

title: Moving Through Clutter: Scaling Data Collection and Benchmarking for 3D Scene-Aware Humanoid Locomotion via Virtual Reality
summary: Recent advances in humanoid locomotion have enabled dynamic behaviors such as dancing, martial arts, and parkour, yet these capabilities are predominantly demonstrated in open, flat, and obstacle-free settings. In contrast, real-world environments such as homes, offices, and public spaces, are densely cluttered, three-dimensional, and geometrically constrained, requiring scene-aware whole-body coordination, precise balance control, and reasoning over spatial constraints imposed by furniture and household objects. However, humanoid locomotion in cluttered 3D environments remains underexplored, and no public dataset systematically couples full-body human locomotion with the scene geometry that shapes it. To address this gap, we present Moving Through Clutter (MTC), an opensource Virtual Reality (VR) based data collection and evaluation framework for scene-aware humanoid locomotion in cluttered environments. Our system procedurally generates scenes with controllable clutter levels and captures embodiment-consistent, whole-body human motion through immersive VR navigation, which is then automatically retargeted to a humanoid robot model. We further introduce benchmarks that quantify environment clutter level and locomotion performance, including stability and collision safety. Using this framework, we compile a dataset of 348 trajectories across 145 diverse 3D cluttered scenes. The dataset provides a foundation for studying geometry-induced adaptation in humanoid locomotion and developing scene-aware planning and control methods.

AI.tldr: MTC is a VR-based framework for collecting and evaluating scene-aware humanoid locomotion data in cluttered 3D environments, addressing the gap between current humanoid capabilities in open spaces and real-world cluttered settings.
AI.motivation: Current humanoid locomotion research focuses on open, flat environments, but real-world settings like homes and offices are densely cluttered and geometrically constrained, requiring scene-aware whole-body coordination and balance control that remains underexplored.
AI.method: Developed a VR-based data collection framework that procedurally generates cluttered scenes with controllable clutter levels, captures whole-body human motion through immersive VR navigation, and automatically retargets motion to humanoid robot models.
AI.result: Created a dataset of 348 trajectories across 145 diverse 3D cluttered scenes, with benchmarks quantifying environment clutter level and locomotion performance metrics including stability and collision safety.
AI.conclusion: MTC provides a foundational dataset and evaluation framework for studying geometry-induced adaptation in humanoid locomotion and developing scene-aware planning and control methods for real-world applications.

title: RODEO: RObotic DEcentralized Organization
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (2026)
summary: Robots are improving their autonomy with minimal human supervision. However, auditable actions, transparent decision processes, and new human-robot interaction models are still missing requirements to achieve extended robot autonomy. To tackle these challenges, we propose RODEO (RObotic DEcentralized Organization), a blockchain-based framework that integrates trust and accountability mechanisms for robots. This paper formalizes Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) for service robots. First, it provides a ROS-ETH bridge between the DAO and the robots. Second, it offers templates that enable organizations (e.g., companies, universities) to integrate service robots into their operations. Third, it provides proof-verification mechanisms that allow robot actions to be auditable. In our experimental setup, a mobile robot was deployed as a trash collector in a lab scenario. The robot collects trash and uses a smart bin to sort and dispose of it correctly. Then, the robot submits a proof of the successful operation and is compensated in DAO tokens. Finally, the robot re-invests the acquired funds to purchase battery charging services. Data collected in a three day experiment show that the robot doubled its income and reinvested funds to extend its operating time. The proof validation times of approximately one minute ensured verifiable task execution, while the accumulated robot income successfully funded up to 88 hours of future autonomous operation. The results of this research give insights about how robots and organizations can coordinate tasks and payments with auditable execution proofs and on-chain settlement.

AI.tldr: RODEO is a blockchain-based framework that integrates trust and accountability mechanisms for service robots through Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), enabling auditable robot actions, transparent decision processes, and automated payment coordination between robots and organizations.
AI.motivation: Current robot autonomy lacks auditable actions, transparent decision processes, and appropriate human-robot interaction models. There is a need for trust and accountability mechanisms to achieve extended robot autonomy in real-world applications.
AI.method: Proposed RODEO framework formalizes DAOs for service robots with three key components: 1) ROS-ETH bridge connecting robots to the DAO, 2) templates for organizations to integrate robots, and 3) proof-verification mechanisms for auditable robot actions. Implemented in a trash collection scenario where robots submit operation proofs for token compensation and reinvest funds for services.
AI.result: In a 3-day experiment, the robot doubled its income and reinvested funds to extend operating time. Proof validation took approximately one minute, ensuring verifiable task execution. Accumulated robot income successfully funded up to 88 hours of future autonomous operation.
AI.conclusion: RODEO demonstrates how robots and organizations can coordinate tasks and payments with auditable execution proofs and on-chain settlement, providing insights into blockchain-based trust and accountability mechanisms for extended robot autonomy.

title: Multimodal Behavior Tree Generation: A Small Vision-Language Model for Robot Task Planning
summary: Large and small language models have been widely used for robotic task planning. At the same time, vision-language models (VLMs) have successfully tackled problems such as image captioning, scene understanding, and visual question answering. In this work, we combine these two approaches by deploying a compact, open-source multimodal model to generate behavior trees for robotic task planning.
